title: The Days on Which Blades Sleep
summary: A seasonal truce protects agricultural work but becomes a contest over credit, staged benevolence, and the manufacture of exemplary lives.

entries.title: Halen of the Shared Oven
entries.body:
Halen’s comedy gave three quarreling neighbors equal time to explain a broken oven. Patrons commissioned a revised ending praising one founder. She performed both versions, making sponsorship visible and protecting audiences from confusing a paid conclusion with the whole story.

Later accounts make Halen of the Shared Oven the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Days on Which Blades Sleep. Coastal feuds in 1007 threatened harvests more severely than either side’s raids. Kitchens, clerics, and net crews negotiated days on which armed retinues could not enter working grounds. A stage performer made the agreement memorable through a domestic comedy about neighbors sharing a broken oven. A celebrated financial adviser later pooled the truce’s guarantees, making compensation available quickly but transferring risk to villages unable to inspect the accounts. Public biographies credited the performer, adviser, or cleric according to the patron commissioning them. Comparing household evidence revealed collective participation and several preventable exclusions. The truce survived because ordinary crews revised it when celebrated founders failed to anticipate changing needs.

In the connected record, [The Blade Resting Green](b009-the-blade-resting-green.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Named Work Protection](b009-the-named-work-protection.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether the guarantee pool can honor small households’ claims before wealthy patrons withdraw the resources securing them.
entries.background: Istren’s fishing villages and timber monasteries occupy a rainy coast where repairing roofs is a continuing expense rather than a finished achievement. Boats make neighboring settlements accessible when inland tracks become mud. Smokehouses, net yards, and communal ovens provide the places where people exchange reliable news. The dead are remembered through finite promises attached to landing water and particular working seasons. A claim on an abandoned beach can become dangerous when erosion moves a new household into its reach. Islanders generally test an alleged manifestation against wind, rot, and tides before paying for an interpreter.

entries.title: The Blade Resting Green
entries.body:
Retinues leave weapons beyond this working meadow on protected days. The boundary follows harvest access, not a holy circle. Nearby fishers petitioned to extend it to net repairs, exposing the agricultural assumptions within a truce advertised as protection for all labor.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Harvest Guarantee Pool
entries.body:
Households contribute grain or pledged repair days to compensate protected-work violations. Large patrons obtain influence through bigger pledges. Small claimants now demand a public order of payment, since nominal generosity offers little protection if wealthy withdrawals empty the store first.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The First Seven Quiet Days
entries.body:
The initial truce covered seven harvest days and excluded night work. Raiders shifted attacks after dusk. Kitchen testimony documented the consequence and helped amend the terms, demonstrating that failure could guide revision rather than discredit the entire attempt.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Comedy’s Broken Oven Door
entries.body:
Its hinge breaks at a rehearsed moment, allowing neighbors to blame each other. Repairs reveal practical knowledge shared between performer and smith. A shrine custodian wants it displayed motionless, removing the mechanical uncertainty that made the scene intelligible.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Unarmed Repair Supper
entries.body:
Opposing crews repair a damaged tool before sharing food. The custom works only when dangerous work is supervised. Wealthy visitors prefer symbolic knots to actual repair, prompting hosts to distinguish courtesy from a contribution that reduces somebody’s burden.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Life of One Peacemaker
entries.body:
This commissioned biography credits a cleric with the truce while naming laborers only as a grateful crowd. An appended provisioning account identifies specific proposals made by cooks and fishers. Readers can now compare the elegant life with its excluded dependencies.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Smokehouse Roof Marten
entries.body:
Martens shelter above warm smokehouses and sometimes steal fish. Feuding households blamed enemy familiars for losses. Joint roof inspection located ordinary nests, creating one small cooperation before formal negotiators succeeded in limiting the more consequential human raids.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Truce Net Path
entries.body:
The path permits unarmed crews to move between protected repair yards. Guards repeatedly treat empty weapon belts as evidence of disguise. A shared token system protects access, but migrants lacking registered households remain dependent upon sponsors willing to vouch for them.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Named Work Protection
entries.body:
Protection attaches to listed work and access routes rather than social rank. Retinue leaders seek exceptions for their own servants. The amended clause counts those servants as workers first, preventing a lord’s quarrel from automatically cancelling their protected day.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Guarantee Shortfall
entries.body:
A storm destroyed pledged timber just as several violation claims arrived. Patrons offered speeches instead of substitute materials. Small households preserved the pool through emergency labor, then demanded voting rights matching the responsibility they had actually assumed.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Pledged Repair Hammer
entries.body:
A hammer passed among compensation crews is remembered as a founder’s relic. Its handle bears later users’ marks. Removing those marks would improve its ceremonial appearance while erasing evidence that the truce survived through people outside the founder’s celebrated lifetime.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Audience’s Other Ending
entries.body:
Audiences propose practical endings after Halen’s comedy, sometimes exposing a settlement that would starve an unseen servant. Performers record those objections. Sponsors dislike the unpredictable interval, but it has supplied revisions more useful than their commissioned verses.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Names Beneath the Crowd
entries.body:
This booklet expands anonymous festival crowds into documented workers. Its compiler leaves uncertain identities unresolved. Families value the recognition while disagreeing about relatives’ motives, preserving a collective history without inventing a uniformly virtuous people.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Quiet Day Pressure
entries.body:
A landing bowl rises slightly during protected days when weapons enter its drain’s reach. Custodians test concealed loads and discover some false accusations. The effect can indicate a material intrusion without identifying who carried it or why.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Truce Tool Repair
entries.body:
Repair crews earn credit for usable work, not hours ceremonially present. Assessing usefulness requires expertise patrons sometimes undervalue. Skilled women and migrants have won witness standing by documenting repairs that official household heads could neither perform nor judge.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Founder Credit Hearing
entries.body:
Three patrons claim exclusive founding honors and a share of festival income. Working crews request money for roof repairs instead. The hearing compares proposals, labor, and surviving accounts, asking what recognition can accomplish beyond financing another persuasive biography.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
